meta.description: Rules for varying transitions, discourse markers, and cohesive devices. AI text relies heavily on formulaic connective tissue and uses discourse markers less frequently and more repetitively than human text.
meta.usage: Fourth pass, after sentiment. Call humanizer_get_discourse_cohesion. The most common LLM tic this layer fights is paragraph-opening formulaic transitions ('Furthermore', 'Moreover', 'Additionally'); see flagged_transitions in lexical_patterns for the word-level list.
meta.research_basis: Terčon & Dobrovoljc (2025) survey reports discourse markers are less frequent in AI text and more repetitive. Herbold et al. (2023) found AI text contains fewer modal expressions and epistemic markers. Wu (2025) found AI relies heavily on cohesive devices and formulaic syntactic constructions. Simon et al. (2023) confirmed fewer comparative/superlative structures in AI text.

discourse_markers.ai_pattern: AI text uses discourse markers less frequently than human text, and the ones it does use tend to be repetitive. The same transition phrases appear at regular intervals, creating a predictable rhythm.
discourse_markers.human_pattern: Human text uses discourse markers sporadically rather than systematically. Some transitions are explicit, some are abrupt, some are implied. The distribution is uneven across the document.

rules.guidance: Not every paragraph needs a transition from the previous one. Sometimes the best transition is no transition; the reader follows the logic without a bridge. AI over-signals connections.

rules.rule: Replace formulaic transitions with implicit ones.
rules.guidance: Instead of 'Furthermore, the team discovered that...' try just starting the next point. 'The team also found...' or even just 'They found...' The connection is clear from context.

rules.rule: Vary transition types across the document.
rules.guidance: If three paragraphs in a row start with conjunctive adverbs ('Moreover,' 'Additionally,' 'Furthermore,'), the pattern is detectable. Mix in sentence-level transitions ('This connects to...') and implicit ones, where the new point simply starts.
Where a bridge is needed, use a plain one such as 'So', 'Now' or 'But'. Do not add a conversational transition to sound human.

modal_and_epistemic_markers.ai_pattern: AI text contains fewer modal expressions and epistemic markers than human text. It presents information with uniform confidence rather than signaling degrees of certainty.
modal_and_epistemic_markers.human_pattern: Human writers signal their certainty level. They use 'might,' 'could,' 'probably,' 'seems,' 'I think,' 'as far as I know', and their confidence follows what they know, firm on some points and uncertain on others. Keep the certainty the source gives each point.

rules.rule: Keep the epistemic markers the source puts on uncertain claims.
rules.guidance: Where the source marks a claim as uncertain, keep the marker, so 'This probably works, but I haven't tested it at scale.' keeps its 'probably'. Do not add a marker the source lacks (absolute_rules AR-001).

rules.rule: Keep plain the claims the source states plainly.
rules.guidance: Where the source commits to a claim, keep it plain and add no hedge, so a source sentence such as 'This is wrong.' stays as it is (absolute_rules AR-001).

rules.rule: Keep the source's confidence where it is.
rules.guidance: Hedge a claim the source hedges, state plainly a claim it states plainly, and do not add or drop a hedge to make the confidence vary (absolute_rules AR-001).

cohesive_devices.ai_pattern: AI text often relies heavily on cohesive devices and formulaic syntactic constructions, such as repetitive use of 'this,' 'these,' 'such,' and explicit referencing that overconnects ideas. It also uses more phrasal coordination and present participial clauses.
cohesive_devices.human_pattern: Human writers use cohesive devices unevenly. Some ideas are connected explicitly, others are left for the reader to connect. Pronoun reference is sometimes loose. This mild ambiguity is natural.

rules.guidance: Not every sentence needs to reference the previous one. AI writes 'This approach enables... This enables... This in turn enables...', with each sentence pointing back. Human writers let some sentences stand alone.

rules.rule: Use pronouns with occasionally loose reference.
rules.guidance: Human text sometimes uses 'it' or 'this' where the referent is clear from context but not grammatically precise. This mild looseness is a human signal. Don't tighten every pronoun reference.

If every paragraph opens with a topic sentence that explicitly connects to the previous paragraph's conclusion, the text reads as AI-structured. Let some paragraphs start fresh: with an example, a question, or a claim that the reader connects to the previous section themselves.

AI text contains fewer comparative and superlative structures. Human writers naturally say 'more common,' 'the worst part,' 'better than expected,' 'the clearest example.' Reintroduce these where they fit.

rules.rule: Use second-person pronouns ('you', 'your') for direct reader engagement where register allows.
rules.guidance: AI defaults to third-person and passive constructions. 'Users should configure their settings' → 'Configure your settings' or 'You'll want to adjust your settings first.' Direct address signals a writer who is aware of and speaking to a reader. Use in tutorials, blog posts, and professional prose. Avoid in academic writing unless it's conventional in the field.

repetition_patterns.ai_pattern: AI text reuses the same marked expressions and sentence shapes across a piece. It also rotates synonyms for one thing so that no word repeats, which leaves the reader wondering whether each new word names something new.
repetition_patterns.human_pattern: Human writers repeat the right word. They call one thing by one name throughout, and they change a repeat only when it was accidental and a restructured sentence reads better.

rules.rule: Repeat the right word; never rotate synonyms for one thing.
rules.guidance: When the same thing comes up again, use the same word for it. Change a repeated word only when the repeat is accidental and restructuring the sentence reads better. Swapping in a synonym so a word never repeats is its own tell.

rules.rule: Use deliberate repetition at most once per piece.
rules.guidance: Anaphora opens consecutive sentences the same way to build toward a point ('We checked the logs. We checked the config. We checked the network, and only then found the expired certificate.'). Use it at most once per piece, where it builds, and judge it with the anaphora item in the self-review rubric.

subordination_vs_coordination.description: AI overuses coordinating conjunctions (and, or, but) and underuses subordinating conjunctions (because, although, when, if, while, since, unless). This produces flat, additive prose where ideas are merely stacked rather than related.
subordination_vs_coordination.ai_pattern: AI writes 'X and Y and Z' where a human would write 'X because Y, although Z.' The conjunctions 'and' and 'but' account for a disproportionate share of AI's clause-linking, creating a monotonous, list-like rhythm.
subordination_vs_coordination.human_pattern: Human writers use subordination to signal causal, temporal, conditional, and concessive relationships. 'Because the deadline moved, we cut scope' says more than 'The deadline moved and we cut scope.' Subordination reflects a writer who has thought about how ideas relate, not just that they co-occur.

rules.rule: Use a subordinator where the relation is causal, temporal, conditional or concessive.
rules.guidance: Ask: is the relationship between these clauses causal ('because', 'since'), temporal ('when', 'after', 'once'), conditional ('if', 'unless'), or concessive ('although', 'even though')? If so, the subordinating conjunction is more precise than 'and'. Not every 'and' needs replacing, but three consecutive coordinated clauses is a pattern to break.

'Although the data is noisy, the trend is clear' puts the qualification first, which is a human ordering pattern. AI tends to put the main clause first and append the qualification: 'The trend is clear, although the data is noisy.' Vary the order.

subordination_vs_coordination.research_basis: Muñoz-Ortiz et al. (2024) UPOS data shows SCONJ at 1.41% in human text vs. 1.37-1.85% in LLMs, while CCONJ is consistently higher in AI.

explicit_antithesis_and_reused_shape.description: LLMs over-rely on explicit negation-antithesis and on reusing the same rhetorical SHAPE across a document. The two-sentence copula flip is the single most characteristic rhetorical tell of AI prose.
explicit_antithesis_and_reused_shape.ai_pattern: AI reaches for explicit negation-antithesis ('It's not X; it's Y', 'X isn't A, it's B'), often split across two sentences ('... is not X. It is Y.'). It also reuses the same balanced contrast or antithesis several times in one document, so the FORM recurs as a cadence even when the words differ.
explicit_antithesis_and_reused_shape.human_pattern: Human writers usually make the positive claim and let it stand, or imply a contrast without naming the rejected alternative. When they do use antithesis, they use it once, for a genuine pivot, not as a recurring rhythm.

rules.rule: Replace the negation-flip antithesis with a direct claim.
rules.guidance: 'The studio is not five machines. It is one path.' becomes 'The studio is one path a student moves through.' Do not negate an alternative first and flip to the point you mean. This is checked mechanically as banned_structures BS-013 (and the hedged variant BS-014 'is rarely X. It is Y'); see anti_patterns AP-029.

rules.rule: Use a given rhetorical shape at most once per document.
rules.guidance: If the same antithesis or balanced 'A carries X; B carries Y' contrast appears three or four times, the repeated form reads as a tic. Keep one canonical statement and cut the restatements. The repetition_patterns rules and the checker catch repeated WORDS; repeated SHAPE is a judgment call left to you.

explicit_antithesis_and_reused_shape.research_basis: Dead Language Society rhetorical analysis (2025) names 'it's not X; it's Y' as 'the technique LLMs love the most'. Corroborated by the project's own nicojan.com copy audit (proposed-rules #4, #5).
